analysis.investment_thesis: Aadhar Housing Finance is a decent affordable-housing lender with 33% PAT CAGR over six years and an ROE that just clears my 15% hurdle, serving the vast underpenetrated low-income segment in India. At 20.8x trailing P/E and 16.2x forward P/E it is priced fairly but not cheaply enough for me to act given the inherent leverage.
key_strengths: Exceptional net profit CAGR of 33.4% over six years (INR 162 Cr → INR 912 Cr), driven by disciplined spread management
ROE of 16.9% slightly exceeds my 15% minimum, supported by improving operating income (21% CAGR over 3 years)
Massive addressable market in affordable housing finance with 64.9% promoter skin in the game
key_risks: Debt/Equity of 2.55x — while normal for an HFC, it means any funding squeeze or NPA cycle hits equity hard
Operating cash flow has been negative every year for five years (-INR 3,027 Cr in 2025); growth entirely dependent on continued borrowing markets
ROCE of only 11.4% suggests capital deployment is not particularly efficient at the business level
red_flags: Persistent negative free cash flow (-INR 3,041 Cr in 2025) is structurally acceptable for HFCs but leaves no margin for error if credit markets tighten
P/B of 3.11x offers limited downside protection if asset quality deteriorates in the affordable segment
No visible data on NPA/GNPA ratios — credit quality is the single most important metric for an HFC and cannot be assessed here
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Aadhar Housing Finance occupies the right end of the Indian housing market — low-ticket, self-employed borrowers in Tier 2-3 towns, a segment that is genuinely underserved and carries long runway. The profit trajectory (INR 162 Cr in 2019 to INR 912 Cr in 2025) is impressive, and the forward P/E of 16.2x is not unreasonable for that growth rate. Finance costs have been disciplined (8.2% CAGR vs 16.1% revenue CAGR), indicating healthy spread preservation.

The stumbling block from my vantage point is leverage: D/E of 2.55x means a small deterioration in asset quality can disproportionately impair book value. I cannot assess moat durability without NPA data; affordable housing lenders compete fiercely on rate and processing speed rather than brand loyalty. At current pricing I would watch and not act — this becomes interesting at 13–15x earnings if the loan book quality proves sound.
